chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from more than one, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Isma'il ibn al-Fadl al-Hashimi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who rented land from the land of the Ahl al-Dhimma (people of the covenant) from the khaj (land tax), and its people were reluctant, and the Sultan only accepted it because of their inability to manage it or despite their ability. He said: 'If the owners are unable to manage it, you may take it, unless they cause you harm. And if you give them something and their souls are pleased with you, then take it.'

He said: And I asked him about a man who bought land from the khaj land, building in it or not, except that some people from the Ahl al-Dhimma settled in it. Is he entitled to take the rent of the houses from them if they pay the jizyah of their heads? He said: 'Make a condition with them, and whatever he takes after the condition is halal.'
And Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar wrote to Abu Muhammad al-Hasan ibn Ali (peace be upon him):

About a man who bought a house from a man in his courtyard with all its rights, and above it is another house. Does the upper house enter into the rights of the lower house or not? So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'He has only what he bought by its name and location, if God wills.'

key_terms.أَهْلُ الذِّمَّةِ: People of the covenant (non-Muslims living under Muslim rule)

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for a Muslim to buy and rent out land from non-Muslims in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the principles of *kharaj* (land tax) and *jizya* (poll tax) in Shia jurisprudence, emphasizing that ownership rights are contingent upon the actual capacity of the *Ahl al-Dhimma* to manage the land and pay dues, rather than mere nominal possession. The ruling on vertical property rights (*haqq al-shurf* or specific inclusion) reflects the Shia emphasis on precise contractual stipulations (*shurut*) in commercial transactions, ensuring that rights are not assumed but explicitly defined. These details highlight the pragmatic approach of the Imams in balancing fiscal administration with the protection of non-Muslim residents' rights under Islamic rule.
